entries.title: Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?
entries.summary: The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.
entries.content:
October 12, 2026

The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.

At under 3 cm (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.

In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.

What we know so far

All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."

That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.

Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.

But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.

This "dilemma" rests in part on the fact that biopsies — removing a small sample of tissue from the spot or nodule to determine whether it's malignant (cancerous) — are difficult to perform on small nodules.

At the same time, the risks involved in a surgical diagnosis are considered "excessive compared to the relatively low prevalence of malignancy in the small nodules." That's according to a 2017 paper published in the European Respiratory Review. And that may also be the dilemma that Pope Leo's doctors have faced.

Fortunately, however, many — if not most — early-stage lung nodules are benign. It is also possible to have more than one nodule at a time, and they can all be benign.

It's said the pope will need a week to recover after his operation to remove the lung nodule. He is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru between November 6-17.

What are lung nodules?

Lung nodules are generally defined as a white spot or lesion on the lung. They have a rounded or irregular shape.

Radiologists refer to their "opacity" because, compared to the surrounding air-filled lung tissue, lung nodules appear as white or gray spots on a CT scan — that is, they have a certain density.

Causes and symptoms of lung nodules

Lung nodules can be caused by old lung infections, foreign particles that are inhaled and get lodged in the lung, inflammation, scar tissue and indeed the onset of cancer.

At more than 3 cm, the nodule is defined as a mass. The bigger it gets, the greater the chance that it will obstruct your airway and the lung's ability to function.

Symptoms may start with chest pain, shortness of breath and wheezing. They may then progress to a chronic cough or coughing up of blood, fatigue, hoarseness, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia.

What makes lung nodules cancerous?

It is hard to determine when lung nodules become life-threatening cancer. But one indicator of a lung nodule's malignancy is its size.

At 2 mm or smaller the risk of cancer is very small and remains so up to a nodule size of about 6-7 mm.

The risk of cancer becomes 9-10% at about 8 to 10 mm. And at larger than 1 cm, the risk of cancer is about 15%.

The density of a lung nodule is also a vital indicator of malignancy.

There are two main categories of lung nodule density: solid and subsolid. Subsolid nodules are further divided into pure ground-glass (nonsolid) and part-solid nodules.

According to a 2026 review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, subsolid nodules are less prevalent than solid nodules, but they have "a higher likelihood of being malignant."

Lung nodules and lung cancer are common

It is said that radiologists see lung nodules in about 30% of chest CT scans. But that number may be rising.

A Dutch study published in 2023 cited an increase in lung nodule detections from 38% of scans in 2008 to 50% in 2019. The same study said "the proportion of patients in whom significant new nodules (≥ 5 mm) were reported increased from 9% in 2010 to 17% in 2017."

However, this may also be a result of the development of better scanning technology in recent years and the use of artificial intelligence to spot tumors.

Bearing in mind that most lung nodules are benign, lung cancer does tend to start with a lesion or nodule. And lung cancer remains the most common type of cancer and the most common cause of cancer death in the world.

The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer says that in 2024 almost 2.65 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 1.8 million people died from the disease.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat over North Korean POWs?
entries.summary: Seoul and Kyiv are trading accusations after the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea. The South insists the move was to be kept secret as it seeks to avoid antagonizing Pyongyang.
entries.content:
South Korea

Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat?

October 12, 2026

Seoul and Kyiv are trading accusations after the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea. The South insists the move was to be kept secret as it seeks to avoid antagonizing Pyongyang.

South Korea's ambassador to Kyiv returned to Seoul on Saturday, his recall the latest in a series of tit-for-tat actions that have severely strained bilateral ties.

The sudden deterioration in their relationship can be traced back to September 23, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly in New York that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.

The soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in the Russian Kursk region in January 2025 as they fought alongside Russian troops.

The South Korean government immediately expressed its anger at Zelenskyy's revelation, insisting that the two governments had reached an agreement to keep the transfer of the two men in mid-September a secret.

Kyiv hit back, by saying that no confidentiality agreement had been in place, to which South Korea accused Ukraine of effectively lying and demanded an official explanation and an apology.

Ukraine has attempted to smooth over what it has called a "diplomatic understanding," but stopped short of the public apology that was expected in Seoul.

Then, reports emerged last week that a close adviser to Zelenskyy had said that more than 176,000 tons of diesel and other energy products were shipped to Russia from South Korean ports in July and August of this year, which would be a breach of international sanctions.

The office of president Lee Jae Myung in Seoul denied the accusation, and two days later recalled its ambassador to Kyiv.

What is behind Seoul's need for secrecy?

There are several reasons why South Korea wanted to keep the POW transfer secret, Erwin Tan, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University, told DW.

"The first was that revealing that the POWs had been repatriated to South Korea would result in Pyongyang retaliating against the families of the men for surrendering," Tan said.

"Seoul also wanted to maintain a channel for communication with Pyongyang," Tan said. "This is a major consideration for the left-leaning wing of Korean politics, which includes President Lee and has historically favored seeking rapprochement with the North."

Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation, agrees that the South Korean government wanted to avoid "friction" with the North.

But Kim pointed out that it was always very likely that both Moscow and Pyongyang would find out about the transfer sooner or later and that Lee was being criticized in some quarters at home for appearing weak.

"There is criticism that Lee's administration is effectively appeasing the North, that it has become too soft, and that is a very worrisome situation," Kim said. Yet he admits to being surprised at how quickly the issue escalated.

"I think Lee was very angry that he was publicly being accused of lying about the agreement and it rapidly grew into a very messy confrontation," he said.

Has Zelenskyy's approach backfired?

While it is unclear why Zelenskyy used his high-profile UN speech to announce the repatriation of the two POWs, Kim believes it may have been a calculated move to win more support from Seoul.

Kyiv could have carried out a prisoner swap with the Russians and won the freedom of some of its own men in return.

But, Kim pointed out, Ukraine instead chose to accede to Seoul's request in the hope that South Korea would respond with additional financial and possibly even military support. That move appears to have backfired.

Professor Tan anticipates that the two governments will continue to "vent steam" over the issue.

"Given the high profile nature of the mutual accusations, both sides will probably engage in a mutual blame game for the immediate future, but I doubt that it will turn into a long-term case of mutual acrimony," he said.

"I anticipate that after the furor has died down and the press is looking for the next new story, both sides will quietly resume contact on the basis of mutual pragmatism."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Cyprus closer than ever to joining Schengen but political hurdles relating to the Green Line and British Sovereign Base Areas remain
entries.summary: The European Commission says Cyprus is ready to join the Schengen Area. Yet questions relating to the island's division and British military bases could still complicate its path to Europe's border-free travel zone.
entries.content:
Cyprus

Cyprus: Green Line complicates island's Schengen ambitions

October 12, 2026

The European Commission says Cyprus is ready to join the Schengen Area. Yet questions relating to the island's division and British military bases could still complicate its path to Europe's border-free travel zone.

Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.

Together with Ireland, Cyprus is currently the only member of the European Union not to be part of Europe's border-free travel zone.

After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.

The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation. Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.

On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."

According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.

Austria, the Netherlands express reservations

However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.

Accession requires a unanimous decision by the EU Council following consultation with the European Parliament.

According to information obtained by DW, Austria and the Netherlands have already informally expressed reservations over security concerns linked to the Green Line, which divides the island of Cyprus, and the special status of the British Sovereign Base Areas.

Although neither country has officially threatened to veto Cyprus's accession, their reservations carry particular weight.

Both Austria and the Netherlands have previously raised objections to the expansion of the Schengen Area to Bulgaria and Romania.

What is the Green Line?

Perhaps the most significant obstacle is the Green Line, the approximately 180-kilometer-long (112 miles) ceasefire line that has divided Cyprus since Turkey's military intervention in 1974.

It separates the areas controlled by the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus from the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island.

The buffer zone is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), while the Green Line itself is not an internationally recognized state border.

Crossings between the two sides take place at nine designated crossing points and are governed by a special EU regulation.

This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line. At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.

"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line. It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.

"For it to be considered to have full control, something would have to change. Either the Cyprus problem would have to be resolved, or a strictly controlled physical border would have to be established. There is no other way," said Hadjigeorgiou.

Why are the British Sovereign Base Areas an issue?

Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.

Together, the two areas cover 254 square kilometers (98 square miles), almost 3% of the island, and remain British sovereign territory.

The main complication concerns the Dhekelia base area, which borders both the territory controlled by the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is not internationally recognized.

Two crossing points, at Pergamos and Strovilia, are located in this area, where checks are carried out by British authorities. The UK is no longer a member of the European Union.

Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou explains the difficulties arising from this unusual arrangement: "This is problematic because the area in question is controlled on one side by the authorities in the occupied north and on the other by the British Sovereign Base Areas."

"As a result, the United Kingdom would be controlling who enters and leaves the Schengen Area. This is an unusual situation, since it is normally the Schengen member states themselves that decide who can enter and leave the area," she said.

According to information obtained by DW, Nicosia and the British Sovereign Base Areas have already begun discussions on upgrading border control procedures at Pergamos and Strovilia to bring them into line with EU requirements.

Political negotiations with EU countries

In the meantime, Nicosia has stepped up its diplomatic efforts to secure the necessary consensus.

Deputy Minister for Migration Nicholas Ioannides held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Austria, the Netherlands and Finland on October 1 on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg. Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.

Cyprus also secured significant political backing on October 7 during the summit of the nine Mediterranean EU member states (MED9) in Croatia.

In their joint declaration, the leaders welcomed the European Commission's positive assessment and called for the timely completion of Cyprus's accession process.

Nevertheless, diplomatic sources speaking to DW on condition of anonymity cautioned that despite the positive signals, Cyprus's entry into the Schengen Area should by no means be taken for granted.

The same sources consider it highly likely that the EU may choose to wait for the outcome of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem before making a decision that could create additional political and practical complications.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: Ukraine says Russia launched strikes hours after Donald Trump announced an 'energy ceasefire'
entries.summary: Less than 24 hours after Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire," Ukraine reported Russian strikes on the northeastern city of Kharkiv. The Kremlin says it would only consider a one-day ceasefire for an election.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine reports Russian strikes despite Trump 'ceasefire'

October 12, 2026

Less than 24 hours after Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire," Ukraine reported Russian strikes on the northeastern city of Kharkiv. The Kremlin says it would only consider a one-day ceasefire for an election.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said Russia carried out strikes, despite US President Donald Trump claiming a "ceasefire" had been agreed over the weekend.

Trump announced unilaterally on social media on Sunday evening that "both parties" had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" which was "effective immediately."

There was no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from Moscow and Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's claim that the ceasefire was "news for me."

Ukrainian energy facility attacked

On Monday morning, Zelenskyy told the annual Warsaw Security Forum that there had been "Russian ​violations of the energy ​ceasefire announced President Trump" overnight, while the mayor of the northeastern city of Kharkiv reporting at least 12 injuries in attacks on energy facilities.

"It was clear that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.

"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then it must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people," he said via video link, adding that he learned about the apparent ceasefire through the media.

Zelenskyy: Ukraine 'will respond' if no ceasefire

Zelenskyy expressed readiness in principle to back an agreement to refrain from attacks on energy infrastructure, but said such a ceasefire must be backed up by security guarantees.

"This ceasefire, it can work, and it can ​become ⁠a major step toward ending the war if ⁠the ​Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it," he said.

"We are waiting for the ​of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to ​see one specific step the Americans are ready to take.

"If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."

EU: No sign of Russia sticking to ceasefire

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg that the bloc would "welcome the energy ceasefire if it holds" but added: "We haven't yet seen that Russia will also stick to it."

French President Emmanuel Macron also insisted that a "real ceasefire" be "respected by both sides" but said: "I ​have ⁠not noted, over the last 48 ⁠hours, ​any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side."

The Russian government said on Monday that President Putin would only consider a ceasefire for a single day in the event that Ukraine intended to hold a presidential election.

The Kremlin earlier rejected ​a 60-day election ceasefire idea proposed by ⁠President ​Zelenskyy.

"I do not think he deserves a respite," said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Germany's Wadephul calls new EU sanctions 'unprecedented' blow to Russia
entries.summary: The European Union has approved its largest-ever sanctions package against Moscow, targeting more than 1,000 entities tied to the military-industrial complex. The move took place in an EU foreign ministers' meeting.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Germany says new EU sanctions 'unprecedented' blow to Russia

October 12, 2026

The European Union has approved its largest-ever sanctions package against Moscow, targeting more than 1,000 entities tied to the military-industrial complex. The move took place in an EU foreign ministers' meeting.

German foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described a new raft of punitive measures against Russia as an "unprecedented sanction blow" to President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine.

"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said on Monday as EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.

Who do the sanctions target?

It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a post on X that this was "the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war...More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."

"We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she added.

Although he could not attend the Luxembourg meeting due to a party conference in Berlin, Wadephul said: "The message is clear: Russia cannot and will not win this war."

However, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to imply that sanctions need to go even further as the conflict was set to enter its fifth bitter winter.

"This is the moment when the entire West...should show Russia and Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means," he told the Warsaw Security Forum, referring to EU sanctions. "That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia.

What is the latest development in the war?

Russian forces have repeatedly stepped up attacks on Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure every autumn since its invasion, hoping to cripple heating and other necessary utilitiesahead of winter.

US President Donald Trump declared that there was an "energy ceasefire" in place between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had no idea what Trump was referring to and that Russia had continued to target energy facilities unabated.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Saudi Arabia: Deadly Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport fuel fears of wider Middle East conflict
entries.summary: Deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have disrupted flights and raised fears of a wider regional conflict, as the US considers military action.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia raise fears of wider war

Published October 12, 2026last updated October 12, 2026

Deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have disrupted flights and raised fears of a wider regional conflict, as the US considers military action.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Riyadh airport to remain closed until October 17 after weekend Houthi attacks killed 14 people and injured more than 300

  • Airstrikes hit Yemen's capital, Sanaa, with the Houthis blaming Saudi Arabia as fighting escalates

  • US President Donald Trump weighs US military action against the Houthis

Here is a roundup of headlines from the wider Middle East region on Monday, October 12.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Iran offers to mediate as Saudi-Houthi fighting escalates

Iran offers to mediate as Saudi-Houthi fighting escalates

Iran has expressed deep concern over escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthi rebels, offering to help facilitate dialogue.

"We are deeply concerned about the developments taking place in the Arabian Peninsula," Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters on Monday.

He said Tehran was ready "to help facilitate dialogue between the parties."

"We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries," Baqaei added, urging both sides to resolve their differences through talks.

His comments follow Houthi attacks on Riyadh's international airport over the weekend that killed 14 people and injured hundreds.

The Houthis are part of Iran's so-called "Axis of Resistance,"  a network of armed groups that also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iraqi Shiite militias.

Skip next section Oil executives absent from Riyadh energy conference

Oil executives absent from Riyadh energy conference

Several leading oil executives have been dropped from the schedule of the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh, as Saudi Arabia presses ahead with the event despite deadly Houthi attacks on the capital.

The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had been expected to attend, but were absent from the agenda released by organisers on Monday.

"To everyone who travelled to Riyadh, thank you," Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told delegates.

"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said, while acknowledging that the risks had not disappeared.

Prince Abdulaziz also insisted that Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 programme, aimed at diversifying the economy away from oil and attracting international investment, must continue despite the attacks.

Skip next section Riyadh airport closure extended after Houthi attacks

Riyadh airport closure extended after Houthi attacks

Saudi Arabia has extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport following deadly Houthi attacks over the weekend.

The General Authority of Civil Aviation said the extension was necessary to complete safety inspections and assess whether airport facilities were ready to resume operations.

The authority did not specify when the airport would reopen.

The attacks killed 14 people and injured hundreds, causing widespread disruption to air travel.

Skip next section Saudi energy minister vows firm response to Houthi attacks

Saudi energy minister vows firm response to Houthi attacks

Saudi Arabia's Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman has said the recent Houthi attacks have tested the kingdom's infrastructure and resilience, warning that the response must be equally serious.

"For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience," he told an energy conference in Riyadh on Monday.

"Energy security can't be taken for granted," he said. "The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."

The remarks follow a weekend of deadly Houthi attacks on Riyadh's international airport that killed 14 people and injured hundreds, forcing authorities to suspend operations.

The attacks were the deadliest to hit Saudi Arabia in a decade.

Skip next section China condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

China condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

China has condemned recent Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and energy infrastructure, expressing concern over the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned rebels.

"China condemns the attacks that caused heavy casualties and expresses serious concern over the intensification of the conflict," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters on Monday.

Mao urged all sides to avoid further escalation and resolve their differences through dialogue and negotiations.

"We call on relevant parties to avoid taking actions that escalate regional tensions," she said, calling for peace and stability in the region.

Skip next section Airstrikes on Yemen's capital kill one, injure 12

Airstrikes on Yemen's capital kill one, injure 12

Airstrikes on Yemen's capital, Sanaa, have killed one person and injured 12 others, according to the Houthi-run Health Ministry.

Ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said a strike on a salt factory in the Hamadan district killed a man and wounded eight people.

A separate strike on a house injured a woman and three children, he added.

The Iran-aligned Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the attacks, which came amid an escalation in fighting between the two sides.

Saudi Arabia has not commented on the allegations.

The strikes followed a weekend of deadly Houthi attacks on Riyadh's international airport that killed 14 people and injured more than 300.

US President Donald Trump has said he is considering joining Saudi Arabia's military campaign against Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels, raising the prospect of further US involvement in the escalating conflict.

Skip next section Riyadh airport stays shut after deadly Houthi attacks

Riyadh airport stays shut after deadly Houthi attacks

Riyadh's main airport remained closed on Monday following deadly attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels, causing widespread flight cancellations across Saudi Arabia.

Saudi aviation authorities extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport, one of the country's busiest aviation hubs.

Aviation analytics firm Cirium said around 60% of scheduled flights at the airport were listed as cancelled on Monday, although the continued suspension meant further disruption was likely.

The airport cancelled 99.7% of its scheduled flights on Sunday, according to Cirium.

The disruption has spread across Saudi Arabia, with more than a third of scheduled flights nationwide expected to be cancelled on Monday.

International airlines have also suspended services. Germany's Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended its suspension until the end of the month.

The US Federal Aviation Administration has urged American airlines to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's coverage of the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels.

Saudi Arabia is dealing with the aftermath of a series of deadly attacks, including two strikes on Riyadh's international airport over the weekend that killed 14 people.

A missile attack on King Khalid International Airport on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, according to Saudi authorities.

A second strike on Sunday killed a Pakistani national and injured at least 11 others. Saudi authorities also reported damage from an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, near Bahrain and Qatar.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, warning that Saudi airports and airspace were "legitimate targets," except for the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

The group said it had targeted the two airports, a gas plant and an Aramco oil refinery using missiles and drones. Its claims could not be independently verified.

Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia jointly condemned the attacks as a violation of Saudi sovereignty and a threat to civilian safety.

The attacks came amid an escalation in fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen. Saudi Arabia has intensified its airstrikes, while the Houthis have warned that further attacks could follow.

US President Donald Trump said over the weekend that Washington was considering joining Saudi military operations against the Houthis. Iran, meanwhile, offered to help facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

The violence has also caused major disruption beyond the airports, with schools in Riyadh switching to remote learning and international airlines suspending services.

entries.title: Nobel Prize in Economics goes to pair of US economists
entries.summary: Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford got the Nobel for developing economic models that help governments and central banks respond more effectively to booms and recessions.
entries.content:
Sweden

Nobel Prize in Economics goes to pair of US economists

October 12, 2026

Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford got the Nobel for developing economic models that help governments and central banks respond more effectively to booms and recessions.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm announced on Monday.

The pair got the Nobel for their work in microeconomic foundations of stabilization policy, allowing for the development of economic models that help governments and central banks respond more effectively to booms and recessions.

Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York.

"It's a tremendous honor, it's a surprise," Woodford said, addressing the committee by phone from New York on Monday.

Why did Hall and Woodford win the Nobel Prize?

The pair of US scientists were awarded for looking toward microeconomic indicators to inform macroeconomic stabilization policies.

They have based their economic models on a microeconomic foundation, breaking with the longstanding Keynesian models, developed by economist John Maynard Keynes almost a century ago.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences argued that decades of applying the Keynesian models showed their limitations – including in failing to curb unemployment and instead raise inflation.

"The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilization policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired," the academy said in its press release.

Hall and Woodford's model instead demonstrated how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.

"The Laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," said John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.

What else to know about the Nobel Economics prize?

The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel.

Last year's prize was awarded to three business innovation researchers who explained how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies behind.

The Sveriges Riksbank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.

Since the economics prize was not one of the five original Nobel Prizes established by Nobel in his will, some argue that it is not technically not a Nobel Prize.

Nevertheless, it is always presented together with the others on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896.

Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.

This year's prize money is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million or €1.07 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: India news: Opposition parties march to Supreme Court
entries.summary: Intensifying their demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, opposition parties are holding a march to the Supreme Court. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Asia

India news: Opposition parties march to Supreme Court

Published October 12, 2026last updated October 12, 2026

Intensifying their demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, opposition parties are holding a march to the Supreme Court. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Opposition parties are set to hold a protest march to Supreme Court over demands that India's election chief step down
  • Jantar Mantar has been denotified as a designated protest site
  • CJP gives Delhi police ultimatum over fixing a date for protest

Here's a round up of the latest developments from India on Monday, October 12:

Tired of missing our real-time updates?Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section INDIA bloc files petition at Supreme Court

INDIA bloc files petition at Supreme Court

INDIA bloc leader Rahul Gandhi along with opposition leaders Mallikarjun Kharge, Saugata Roy, Akhilesh Yadav and Tejashwi Prasad Yadav filed a petition against the Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls at the Supreme Court.

Skip next section Opposition leaders march to Supreme Court

Opposition leaders march to Supreme Court

Opposition leaders have begun their march from the Barakhamba Road to the Supreme Court in New Delhi, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The leaders were seen in buses leaving from the Constitution Club to the Barakhamba Road in New Delhi.

The Rahul Gandhi-led INDIA alliance has announced that it will also file a petition at the Supreme Court over the issue of the controversial revision of voter rolls that has resulted in mass deletions.

Opposition leader Gandhi and a few others will be allowed to enter the Supreme Court premises to file their petition.

The Supreme Court administration has agreed that five to 10 leaders, accompanied by their lawyers, can file the petition at the filing counter within the court complex, according to a report by Indian newspaper Hindustan Times.

Skip next section CJP asks police to give them new Jantar Mantar protest date within 24 hours

CJP asks police to give them new Jantar Mantar protest date within 24 hours

The Cockroach Janta Partya (CJP) have asked the Delhi police to give them a date within 24 hours to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar . 

CJP leader Ashutosh Ranka has made the call in a post on X, saying that otherwise, the CJP will give another protest call."

On Saturday, the CJP had planned a protest over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. However, the protests were forcefully thwarted and the CJP leaders were detained by the Delhi police.

Skip next section Jantar Mantar delisted as designated protest site

Jantar Mantar delisted as designated protest site

The Delhi Police on Monday announced that Jantar Mantar is no longer a "designated site" for protests. It has instead listed three alternative venues — the Ramlila Ground in Central Delhi, the Burari Ground in North Delhi, and the CBD Ground in East Delhi.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has slammed the move, calling it "unacceptable."

"The Jantar Mantar belongs to THE PEOPLE OF INDIA. Did the Ministry of Home Affairs consult with the people of India? Were any stakeholders consulted? Were any organisations consulted?" CJP leader Saurav Das said in a post on X. "We do not accept this arbitrary decision."

Jantar Mantar has remained an iconic and significant protest site in the country, having witnessed several monumental demonstrations.

The move comes two days after protesters demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar were stopped from entering the protest site amid heavy deployment and barricading.

Since June this year, the site has remained a focal point for youth-led protests spearheaded by the CJP.

Skip next section INDIA bloc to hold protest march demanding CEC's resignation

INDIA bloc to hold protest march demanding CEC's resignation

Leader of the opposition and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi-led INDIA bloc is going to march to the Supreme Court today at 4 p.m. local time (10:30 UTC), intensifying their agitation against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Gandhi urged people to join his "march for democracy" and "march for justice" in a post on X, as he gave the "Chalo Dilli" (Let's go to Delhi) call ahead of the INDIA bloc's planned march to the Supreme Court.

The call for the protest march came a day after forceful, mass detentions of protesters, journalists and lawyers were reported in Delhi on Saturday.

The Cockroach Janta Party has also expressed support for the planned march.

The Congress Party had sought a meeting with the Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant to raise the issue of alleged vote theft.



However, the CJI declined the meeting, reportedly citing the matter being sub judice in the Supreme Court.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Midhat from the Delhi studio, bringing you all the important news emerging from India.

The capital continues to witness chaos as protesters demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation persist despite a clampdown by the Delhi Police on the demonstrations over the weekend.

The protests come after a recent report found that Kumar took unilateral decisions that resulted in mass voter deletions, allegedly in violation of law.

The opposition alliance INDIA bloc plans to march to the Supreme Court. It intends to submit a memorandum to the Chief Justice of India.

Meanwhile, the Delhi Police has announced that Jantar Mantar has been delisted as a designated protest site.

Here's a quick recap of what happened in Delhi over the weekend:

On October 2, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) announced that it will protest at Jantar Mantar — the designated protest site in Delhi – on October 10, demanding Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.

Ahead of the protests, security was beefed up in several parts of Delhi. According to local media reports, over 30,000 security personnel were deployed in Delhi. The internet was suspended within 4 kilometers (2.4 miles) of Jantar Mantar.

On Saturday, the Delhi Police blocked routes to Jantar Mantar to thwart the protests. Roads were lined with buses to detain protesters while parts of Delhi were locked down.

Flash protests emerged in Connaught Place and Safdarjung, where protesters were detained in large numbers and dragged forcefully into buses.

Besides protesters and the CJP leaders, several lawyers and journalists were also reportedly detained by the police.

The police cited a ban on unauthorized public gatherings under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) for the mass detentions.

Stay tuned as we bring you more.

entries.title: Germany's women: Ena Mahmutovic makes her case to become Germany's next No.1 goalkeeper
entries.summary: Germany's win against Australia saw Ena Mahmutovic excel in goal. The 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper is considered the successor to Ann-Katrin Berger and is making a name for herself.
entries.content:
October 12, 2026

Germany's win against Australia saw Ena Mahmutovic excel in goal. The 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper is considered the successor to Ann-Katrin Berger and is making a name for herself.

With determination, pace, and four beautifully crafted goals, Germany's women won its friendly against Australia, thrilling not only the fans but also head coach Christian Wück.

"You can see how fired up the girls are, how well they're already playing together, and that we have an incredible amount of talent on the field and on the bench," said a delighted Wück after his team's well-deserved 4-2 victory.

Since there were several notable absences, including captain Giulia Gwinn and top scorer Lea Schüller, others had to step up and fill the gaps. And they did so with flying colors. Melissa Kössler made a strong case for herself as a striker by scoring her first two international goals. Center back Camilla Küver and Sjoeke Nüsken were also on the scoresheet.

Mahmutovic seizes her chance in goal

Much like it was with the men's team during Jürgen Klopp's first international break as Germany head coach, the question as to who will emerge as the next number one goalkeeper for the women was also a hot topic.

The difference is that unlike Manuel Neuer, who has retired from international football, Ann-Katrin Berger is sticking around for at least one more tournament cycle.

However, with just three matches to go before the start of the playoffs in the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), where she plays for Gotham FC, Berger is giving these two Germany friendlies a miss.

Parallels to men's goalkeeping situation

This means 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper Ena Mahmutovic, who is seen as a potential successor to Berger, took her her chance.

"Ena deserves to play the next match," Wück said ahead of the game. "We must not forget that she already kept a clean sheet in Slovenia (Germany's last World Cup qualifier). And I hope she can repeat that tomorrow."

Some will draw parallels to Jonas Urbig, who many see as a future number one for Germany's men. Both he and Mahmutovic were born in 2003 in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, and both are seen as up-and-coming stars for their club and country. 

The difference is that while Urbig remains an understudy to Neuer at Bayern, Mahmutovic is already the first-choice keeper at her club, having won the starting job over Maria Luisa Grohs prior to the start of the season.

For Germany, though, Mahmutovic still has to bide her time, while there are already strong indications that Klopp intends to make Urbig his number one.

'The future of the national team'

"I'm obviously delighted," Mahmutovic said ahead of the games.

"It's always something special, of course – especially playing against a team from another continent. I think testing ourselves against them is very helpful as we look ahead to the World Cup."

Bayern director Bianca Rech recently described Mahmutovic as "the future of the national team," calling on Wück not only to give her a callup, but also regular playing time.

Wück still sees Berger as slightly better than Mahmutovic, but he is also full of praise for the young keeper.

"Ena's performances have been very good," he said. "She will get her playing time."

Costly mistake in Germany debut

The match against Slovenia was just Mahmutovic's second appearances for Germany. Her first, which came almost two years ago, was memorable for the wrong reason. In the dying minutes of a friendly in December 2024, she lost control of the ball after a back pass, allowing an Italian forward to score the winner in a 2-1 defeat for Germany. Still, Mahmutovic was included in Germany's squad for the 2025 Euros.

Had it been up to her father – who is from Montenegro – Mahmutovic would never have become a goalkeeper.

"He still says I would have been better as an outfield player because I'm good with both feet," she said.

Unusual Bundesliga debut

That's a quality that evidently wasn't lost on Thomas Gerstner, when her coach at her then-club Duisburg, gave her her Women's Bundesliga debut in May 2020. With the team coping with several absences, the then-16-year-old, who had been on the bench as backup goalkeeper, came on as an outfield player.

"The coach brought me on during stoppage time," Mahmutovic recalled. "I got to make two sprints – that was my debut."

That, however, was a one-off, and nobody questions Mahmutovic's strengths as a goalkeeper.

"She is one of the most talented goalkeepers in the world," said Bayern coach Jose Barcala, noting that she is the kind of player who can decide a match.

Mahmutovic will be hoping she gets many more opportunities to do just that for Germany.

This article was originally published in German.

This article was updated on October 12 after Germany's friendly against Australia.

entries.title: Frankfurt Book Fair: Rights lawyer Sands awarded peace prize
entries.summary: Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands was awarded the German Book Trade's Peace Prize this weekend. Accepting the award, Sands criticized Germany's "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel.
entries.content:
October 12, 2026

Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands was awarded the German Book Trade's Peace Prize this weekend. Accepting the award, Sands criticized Germany's "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel.

The 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair concluded on Sunday with the awarding of the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade to the Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands.

Sands was honored in the presence of German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier as a committed humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."

The jury said that his work was based on a "commitment to the universal rights of every human being, evidenced in his advocacy for victims of war crimes, racism, torture and colonial injustice."

Sands criticizes Germany's 'silence' on Israel

Sands, a professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, used his acceptance speech to criticize Germany for what he called its "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel and its actions in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.

Sands said human rights abuses should be clearly named, especially among allies, stating: "It's not antisemitic. It's not anti-Israel. It's the truth."

Sands, himself a descendent of Jews driven out of what is now Lviv in western Ukraine during the German occupation in the Second World War, became known to a broader audience through his 2016 book East West Street: On the Origins of Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity.

The work, which details the lives of two Jewish lawyers, Hersch Lauterpacht and Raphael Lemkin, and the origins of international criminal law, was translated into dozens of languages, including German as Rückkehr nach Lemberg (Return to Lviv) in 2018.

"Germany knows all about ethnic cleansing," Sands said in Frankfurt, referring to criticism leveled at Israel by many states over its treatment of Palestinians.

"So why the silence? Silence is not the way. Not for a family. Not for a community. Not for a country."

Sands also condemned the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, as "appalling" and "a monstrous crime against the norms of international law" and acknowledged that Israel, like any state, has a right to defend itself.

"[But] this right is not unlimited and must be practiced within the boundaries of international law."

Edited by: Rana Taha
